claim: The R-loop is a common transcriptional by-product that consists of an RNA-DNA duplex joined to a displaced strand of genomic DNA.
source: The R-loop is a common transcriptional by-product that consists of an RNA-DNA duplex joined to a displaced strand of genomic DNA.
evidence: This is a definitional statement presented in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about R-loop structure.

claim: The Smc5/6 complex plays a crucial role in the removal of R-loop structures formed during gene transcription.
source: Here, we show that a core regulator of chromosome architecture —the Smc5/6 complex— plays a crucial role in the removal of R-loop structures formed during gene transcription.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by multiple experimental approaches including genetic interactions, RNA-DNA hybrid accumulation assays, and in vitro biochemical experiments.

claim: Budding yeast mutants defective in the Smc5/6 complex and enzymes involved in R-loop resolution show strong synthetic interactions.
source: Consistent with this, budding yeast mutants defective in the Smc5/6 complex and enzymes involved in R-loop resolution show strong synthetic interactions and accumulate high levels of RNA-DNA hybrid structures in their chromosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 4, demonstrating growth defects in double mutants.

claim: Budding yeast mutants defective in the Smc5/6 complex and enzymes involved in R-loop resolution accumulate high levels of RNA-DNA hybrid structures in their chromosomes.
source: Consistent with this, budding yeast mutants defective in the Smc5/6 complex and enzymes involved in R-loop resolution show strong synthetic interactions and accumulate high levels of RNA-DNA hybrid structures in their chromosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by S9.6 immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2 and DRIP-qPCR data in Figure 3A.

claim: The Smc5/6 complex acts on specific types of RNA-DNA hybrid structures in vivo.
source: Importantly, we demonstrate that the Smc5/6 complex acts on specific types of RNA-DNA hybrid structures in vivo and promotes R-loop degradation by the RNase H2 enzyme in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by genetic interaction data in Figure 4 showing specificity for transcription-associated and telomeric R-loops but not replication-associated R-loops.

claim: The Smc5/6 complex promotes R-loop degradation by the RNase H2 enzyme in vitro.
source: Importantly, we demonstrate that the Smc5/6 complex acts on specific types of RNA-DNA hybrid structures in vivo and promotes R-loop degradation by the RNase H2 enzyme in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro biochemical assays shown in Figure 6C demonstrating enhanced RNase H2 activity in the presence of SMC5/6 complex.

claim: The Smc5/6 complex has a crucial role in the removal of toxic R-loops formed at highly transcribed genes and telomeres.
source: Collectively, our results reveal a crucial role for the Smc5/6 complex in the removal of toxic R-loops formed at highly transcribed genes and telomeres.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by genetic interaction data with sen1-1, hpr1Δ, and rat1-1 mutants (Figure 4) and DRIP data showing accumulation at telomeres and rDNA (Figure 3A).

claim: During transcription, nascent RNA transcripts can re-anneal to complementary DNA strands producing an RNA-DNA hybrid and displace the template strand.
source: During transcription, nascent RNA transcripts can re-anneal to complementary DNA strands producing an RNA-DNA hybrid and displace the template strand, creating an obstacle to the progression of the DNA replication machinery.
evidence: This is a mechanistic description of R-loop formation based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: R-loops are highly deleterious for genome integrity.
source: The resulting RNA-DNA hybrid and displaced ssDNA segment —together termed the R-loop— are highly deleterious for genome integrity (Chatzidoukaki et al., 2021; Costantino and Koshland, 2018; De Magis et al., 2019; Stork et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: RNA-DNA hybrid structures can be formed under a variety of physiological conditions in eukaryotic genomes and play important roles in cell physiology and regulate genome dynamics.
source: RNA-DNA hybrid structures can also be formed under a variety of physiological conditions in eukaryotic genomes and play important roles in cell physiology and regulate genome dynamics.
evidence: This is a general statement about RNA-DNA hybrids supported by established scientific knowledge and citations.

claim: RNA-DNA hybrids play a role in immunoglobulin class switching recombination of B cells in vertebrates.
source: Common physiological roles of RNA-DNA hybrids include immunoglobulin class switching recombination of B cells in vertebrates (Yu et al., 2003; Roy et al., 2008), mitochondrial DNA replication (Pohjoismäki et al., 2010; Xu and Clayton, 1996), bacterial plasmid replication (Baker and Kornberg, 1988; McLean et al., 2022), and CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing (Zhang et al., 2021; Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: RNA-DNA hybrids play a role in mitochondrial DNA replication.
source: Common physiological roles of RNA-DNA hybrids include immunoglobulin class switching recombination of B cells in vertebrates (Yu et al., 2003; Roy et al., 2008), mitochondrial DNA replication (Pohjoismäki et al., 2010; Xu and Clayton, 1996), bacterial plasmid replication (Baker and Kornberg, 1988; McLean et al., 2022), and CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing (Zhang et al., 2021; Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: RNA-DNA hybrids play a role in bacterial plasmid replication.
source: Common physiological roles of RNA-DNA hybrids include immunoglobulin class switching recombination of B cells in vertebrates (Yu et al., 2003; Roy et al., 2008), mitochondrial DNA replication (Pohjoismäki et al., 2010; Xu and Clayton, 1996), bacterial plasmid replication (Baker and Kornberg, 1988; McLean et al., 2022), and CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing (Zhang et al., 2021; Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: RNA-DNA hybrids play a role in CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing.
source: Common physiological roles of RNA-DNA hybrids include immunoglobulin class switching recombination of B cells in vertebrates (Yu et al., 2003; Roy et al., 2008), mitochondrial DNA replication (Pohjoismäki et al., 2010; Xu and Clayton, 1996), bacterial plasmid replication (Baker and Kornberg, 1988; McLean et al., 2022), and CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing (Zhang et al., 2021; Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: RNA-DNA hybrids coordinate specific regulatory steps in transcription initiation and termination.
source: Moreover, RNA-DNA hybrids co-ordinate specific regulatory steps in transcription initiation and termination (Sidorenkov et al., 1998; Skourti-Stathaki et al., 2011; Nudler et al., 1997), telomere homeostasis (Balk et al., 2013; Luke et al., 2008), and gene expression (Crossley et al., 2019; García-Muse and Aguilera, 2019; Brambati et al., 2020; Niehrs and Luke, 2020; Zardoni et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: RNA-DNA hybrids coordinate telomere homeostasis.
source: Moreover, RNA-DNA hybrids co-ordinate specific regulatory steps in transcription initiation and termination (Sidorenkov et al., 1998; Skourti-Stathaki et al., 2011; Nudler et al., 1997), telomere homeostasis (Balk et al., 2013; Luke et al., 2008), and gene expression (Crossley et al., 2019; García-Muse and Aguilera, 2019; Brambati et al., 2020; Niehrs and Luke, 2020; Zardoni et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: RNA-DNA hybrids coordinate gene expression.
source: Moreover, RNA-DNA hybrids co-ordinate specific regulatory steps in transcription initiation and termination (Sidorenkov et al., 1998; Skourti-Stathaki et al., 2011; Nudler et al., 1997), telomere homeostasis (Balk et al., 2013; Luke et al., 2008), and gene expression (Crossley et al., 2019; García-Muse and Aguilera, 2019; Brambati et al., 2020; Niehrs and Luke, 2020; Zardoni et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The formation of unprogrammed or non-physiological RNA-DNA hybrid structures can interfere with DNA replication-related processes, resulting in replicative stress and the formation of DNA double-strand breaks.
source: However, the formation of unprogrammed or non-physiological RNA-DNA hybrid structures can interfere with DNA replication-related processes, resulting in replicative stress and the formation of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) (Crossley et al., 2019; Aguilera and García-Muse, 2012; Santos-Pereira and Aguilera, 2015; Hamperl et al., 2017; Kumar et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Exposed ssDNA in the R-loop can be cleaved by different endonucleases leading to DNA breaks and/or mutagenic events.
source: Importantly, exposed ssDNA in the R-loop can be cleaved by different endonucleases leading to DNA breaks and/or mutagenic events, and can also adopt harmful secondary structures (Freudenreich, 2018; Miglietta et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Exposed ssDNA in the R-loop can adopt harmful secondary structures.
source: Importantly, exposed ssDNA in the R-loop can be cleaved by different endonucleases leading to DNA breaks and/or mutagenic events, and can also adopt harmful secondary structures (Freudenreich, 2018; Miglietta et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: R-loop-induced DNA damage and genomic rearrangements have been linked to various disease states in humans including trinucleotide repeat-associated diseases, auto-immune disorders, neurological disorders, and cancer.
source: R-loop-induced DNA damage and genomic rearrangements have been linked to various disease states in humans. Examples include trinucleotide repeat-associated diseases, auto-immune disorders, neurological disorders, and cancer, although it is not currently known whether R-loops play a causative or consequential role in such diseases (García-Muse and Aguilera, 2019; Richard and Manley, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: It is not currently known whether R-loops play a causative or consequential role in human diseases.
source: Examples include trinucleotide repeat-associated diseases, auto-immune disorders, neurological disorders, and cancer, although it is not currently known whether R-loops play a causative or consequential role in such diseases (García-Muse and Aguilera, 2019; Richard and Manley, 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The Ribonuclease H (RNase H) family of enzymes plays a central role in degrading the RNA moiety of R-loops.
source: For instance, the Ribonuclease H (RNase H) family of enzymes plays a central role in degrading the RNA moiety of R-loops created under a variety of genomic conditions (Lazzaro et al., 2012; Lockhart et al., 2019; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The RNase DICER can cleave the RNA moiety of the R-loops in higher eukaryotes.
source: Recently, it was shown that the RNase DICER can also cleave the RNA moiety of the R-loops in higher eukaryotes (Camino et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent literature.

claim: Factors associated with transcription and mRNA biogenesis, RNA-DNA helicases, topoisomerases, chromatin remodelers, and several DNA repair enzymes are involved alongside RNase H in preventing the accumulation of R-loop structures in eukaryotic chromosomes.
source: In addition, factors associated with transcription and mRNA biogenesis, RNA-DNA helicases, topoisomerases, chromatin remodelers, and several DNA repair enzymes are known to be involved alongside RNase H in preventing the accumulation of R-loop structures in eukaryotic chromosomes (García-Muse and Aguilera, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Previous work provides hints of a possible involvement of structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC)-type complexes in RNA-DNA hybrid metabolism.
source: Work from our laboratory and other researchers provides hints of a possible involvement of structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC)-type complexes in RNA-DNA hybrid metabolism (Lafuente-Barquero et al., 2017; Serrano et al., 2020; Girasol et al., 2023; Penzo et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature including work from the authors' laboratory.

claim: SMC complexes are effectors of large-scale changes in chromosome organization and include three evolutionarily conserved enzyme complexes: condensin, cohesin, and the Smc5/6 complex.
source: SMC complexes are effectors of large-scale changes in chromosome organization and include three evolutionarily conserved enzyme complexes: condensin, cohesin, and the Smc5/6 complex (Peng and Zhao, 2023).
evidence: This is a statement about the SMC complex family supported by a citation.

claim: The Smc5/6 complex function is primarily concerned with DNA repair, unlike that of cohesin and condensin.
source: The Smc5/6 complex is a particularly intriguing member of this family because its function —unlike that of cohesin and condensin— is primarily concerned with DNA repair, and yet its exact contribution to this process is not fully understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the known function of Smc5/6 complex based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The Smc5/6 complex is a DNA compacting enzyme that acts in vivo by regulating local chromatin domains containing unusual DNA structures that can lead to replication stress and/or DNA damage.
source: Recent evidence suggests that the Smc5/6 complex is a DNA compacting enzyme that acts in vivo by regulating local chromatin domains containing unusual DNA structures that can lead to replication stress and/or DNA damage (Serrano et al., 2020; Gutierrez-Escribano et al., 2020; Tanasie et al., 2022; Pradhan et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent literature including work from the authors' laboratory.

claim: Genome-wide screens and targeted genetic analyses revealed synthetic interactions among a subset of mutants affecting Smc5/6 complex components and RNA-DNA hybrid detoxification enzymes.
source: Interestingly, genome-wide screens as well as targeted genetic analyses revealed synthetic interactions among a subset of mutants affecting Smc5/6 complex components and RNA-DNA hybrid detoxification enzymes (Lafuente-Barquero et al., 2017; Costanzo et al., 2016; Styles et al., 2016; Kuzmin et al., 2018; Chang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The Smc5/6 complex can bind to short RNA-DNA duplexes with high affinity and specificity.
source: Consistent with this, we have previously shown that the Smc5/6 complex can bind to short RNA-DNA duplexes with high affinity and specificity (Serrano et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work from the authors' laboratory.

claim: In eukaryotes, two partially overlapping enzymes mediate the degradation of R-loops: RNase H1 and RNase H2.
source: In eukaryotes, two partially overlapping enzymes mediate the degradation of R-loops; RNase H1 and RNase H2 (Figure 1A; Lazzaro et al., 2012; Lockhart et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The smc6-9 and nse4-4 alleles correspond to moderate and strong temperature-sensitive mutants of the Smc5/6 complex, respectively.
source: We used the smc6-9 and nse4-4 alleles for our analysis because they correspond to moderate and a strong temperature-sensitive mutants of the Smc5/6 complex, respectively, and inactivate its DNA repair activity in a general/non-specific manner (Ben-Aroya et al., 2008; Hwang et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature characterizing these alleles.

claim: The smc6-9 and nse4-4 alleles inactivate Smc5/6 complex DNA repair activity in a general/non-specific manner.
source: We used the smc6-9 and nse4-4 alleles for our analysis because they correspond to moderate and a strong temperature-sensitive mutants of the Smc5/6 complex, respectively, and inactivate its DNA repair activity in a general/non-specific manner (Ben-Aroya et al., 2008; Hwang et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature characterizing these alleles.

claim: Loss of both Smc5/6 and RNase H activities resulted in impaired proliferation even under optimal growth conditions.
source: Loss of both Smc5/6 and RNase H activities resulted in impaired proliferation even under optimal growth conditions, as illustrated by the growth patterns of haploid spores after sporulation and dissection of heterozygous diploid strains (Figure 1C and D; YPD 23 °C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Double mutant strains defective in Smc5/6 and RNase H exhibit heightened temperature sensitivity at 30 °C and 32 °C compared to their corresponding parental strains.
source: Competitive proliferation assays revealed that double mutant strains exhibit heightened temperature sensitivity at 30 °C and 32 °C compared to their corresponding parental strains (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Yeast cells without RNase H activity can replicate their chromosomes normally under unchallenged growth conditions.
source: Yeast cells without RNase H activity can replicate their chromosomes normally under unchallenged growth conditions, but their replication is hampered when exposed to DNA-damaging agents or replication inhibitors (Lockhart et al., 2019; Heuzé et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Replication of yeast cells without RNase H activity is hampered when exposed to DNA-damaging agents or replication inhibitors.
source: Yeast cells without RNase H activity can replicate their chromosomes normally under unchallenged growth conditions, but their replication is hampered when exposed to DNA-damaging agents or replication inhibitors (Lockhart et al., 2019; Heuzé et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Most of the Smc5/6-RNase H double mutants were more sensitive than single mutant strains when exposed to genotoxic stress.
source: Consistent with this, most of the Smc5/6-RNase H double mutants were more sensitive than single mutant strains when exposed to genotoxic stress (e.g., see HU at 23 °C in Figure 1D; MMS and 4NQO in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Loss of Smc5/6 complex activity in combination with RNase H2 mutations in a RNase H1 proficient background gives rise to a synthetic growth defect.
source: A similar growth exacerbation phenotype was observed when Smc5/6 complex mutations were combined with RNase H2 mutations in a RNase H1 proficient background (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Loss of Smc5/6 complex E3-ligase activity in the mms21-H202Y mutant gives rise to a synthetic growth defect when combined with RNase H mutations.
source: Loss of Smc5/6 complex E3-ligase activity in the mms21-H202Y mutant also gave rise to a synthetic growth defect when combined with RNase H mutations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), thereby implicating sumoylation in RNA-DNA hybrid processing.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Sumoylation is implicated in RNA-DNA hybrid processing.
source: Loss of Smc5/6 complex E3-ligase activity in the mms21-H202Y mutant also gave rise to a synthetic growth defect when combined with RNase H mutations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), thereby implicating sumoylation in RNA-DNA hybrid processing.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic interaction data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A large increase in the numbers of S9.6 foci was detected on chromatin spreads prepared from double mutants compared to those from single mutant strains.
source: Remarkably, we detected a large increase in the numbers of S9.6 foci on chromatin spreads prepared from double mutants compared to those from single mutant strains (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: RNase H mutants alone typically show a few RNA-DNA hybrid/S9.6 foci per nucleus.
source: Whereas RNase H mutants alone typically show a few RNA-DNA hybrid/S9.6 foci per nucleus, inactivating Smc5/6 components in this genetic background resulted in the accumulation of more than 10 foci per nucleus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Inactivating Smc5/6 components in RNase H mutant background resulted in the accumulation of more than 10 S9.6 foci per nucleus.
source: Whereas RNase H mutants alone typically show a few RNA-DNA hybrid/S9.6 foci per nucleus, inactivating Smc5/6 components in this genetic background resulted in the accumulation of more than 10 foci per nucleus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The presence of S9.6 foci was highest in the nse4-4 rnh1Δ rnh201Δ and smc6-9 rnh1Δ rnh201Δ strains.
source: The presence of S9.6 foci was highest in the nse4-4 rnh1Δ rnh201Δ and smc6-9 rnh1Δ rnh201Δ strains, consistent with the fact that rnh201Δ represents the deletion of the catalytic subunit of RNase H2 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: rnh201Δ represents the deletion of the catalytic subunit of RNase H2.
source: The presence of S9.6 foci was highest in the nse4-4 rnh1Δ rnh201Δ and smc6-9 rnh1Δ rnh201Δ strains, consistent with the fact that rnh201Δ represents the deletion of the catalytic subunit of RNase H2 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a statement about the genetic nature of the rnh201Δ mutation based on established knowledge.

claim: RNA-DNA hybrids accumulated to similar levels in RNase H-only mutants (rnh1Δ rnh201Δ, rnh1Δ rnh202Δ, and rnh1Δ rnh203Δ strains carrying 3–10 S9.6 foci per nucleus).
source: RNA-DNA hybrids accumulated to similar levels in RNase H-only mutants (see rnh1Δ rnh201Δ, rnh1Δ rnh202Δ, and rnh1Δ rnh203Δ strains carrying 3–10 S9.6 foci per nucleus; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: nse4-4 and smc6-9 mutations alone did not result in a statistically significant increase in RNA-DNA foci formation.
source: nse4-4 and smc6-9 mutations alone did not result in a statistically significant increase in RNA-DNA foci formation, indicating that cells possess excess R-loop processing capacity when RNase H and other alternate R-loop metabolism pathways are active.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cells possess excess R-loop processing capacity when RNase H and other alternate R-loop metabolism pathways are active.
source: nse4-4 and smc6-9 mutations alone did not result in a statistically significant increase in RNA-DNA foci formation, indicating that cells possess excess R-loop processing capacity when RNase H and other alternate R-loop metabolism pathways are active.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that single Smc5/6 mutants do not accumulate significant RNA-DNA hybrids.

claim: Overexpression of an ectopic copy of RNase H1 gene by galactose induction in the single and double mutant strains largely suppressed the S9.6 signal on chromatin spreads.
source: Importantly, overexpression of an ectopic copy of RNase H1 gene (PGAL1-RNH1) by galactose induction in the single and double mutant strains largely suppressed the S9.6 signal on chromatin spreads (compared to control cells without RNase H1 overexpression; Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The foci detected by S9.6 antibody are reflective of RNA-DNA hybrid formation in double mutant strains.
source: These results indicate that the foci described in Figure 2A are reflective of RNA-DNA hybrid formation in double mutant strains.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNase H1 overexpression experiment shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Increased RNA-DNA hybrid immunoprecipitation was observed specifically at telomeres and ribosomal genes in the Smc5/6-RNase H double mutant strains compared to the parental strains deficient in only RNase H activity.
source: Consistent with the chromosome spread analysis, we observed increased RNA-DNA hybrid immunoprecipitation specifically at telomeres and ribosomal genes in the Smc5/6-RNase H double mutant strains compared to the parental strains deficient in only RNase H activity (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by DRIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The single-stranded DNA region of R-loop structures can be directly targeted by activation-induced cytosine deaminase (AID).
source: Previous studies have established that the single-stranded DNA region of R-loop structures can be directly targeted by various mutagenic enzymes, one of them being the activation-induced cytosine deaminase (AID).
evidence: This claim is supported by prior literature establishing this mechanism.

claim: AID is highly active on single-stranded DNA during active transcription and creates mutations in DNA by deamination of cytosine and converting cytosine into uracil.
source: This enzyme is highly active on single-stranded DNA during active transcription and creates mutations in DNA by deamination of cytosine and converting cytosine into uracil.
evidence: This is a description of AID enzyme activity based on established knowledge.

claim: AID-induced mutations lead to increased Rad52 foci formation in yeast.
source: This event leads to increased Rad52 foci formation in yeast, a homologous recombination-related phenotype that can be exploited to quantify R-loop abundance upon overexpression of the AID enzyme (Cañas et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A substantially higher level of AID-induced Rad52-GFP foci formation was observed in the nse4-4 rnh1Δ rnh201Δ mutant strain compared to a wild-type control or the parental single mutants.
source: In line with our previous results, we observed a substantially higher level of AID-induced Rad52-GFP foci formation in the nse4-4 rnh1Δ rnh201Δ mutant strain compared to a wild-type control or the parental single mutants (rnh1Δ rnh201Δ; Figure 3B, wild-type and nse4-4; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The severe growth defects of yeast defective in both RNase H and the Smc5/6 complex can be linked to an accumulation of R-loops in the chromosomes of these cells.
source: These results suggest that the severe growth defects of yeast defective in both RNase H and the Smc5/6 complex can be linked to an accumulation of R-loops in the chromosomes of these cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence including S9.6 staining, DRIP, and AID-induced Rad52 foci.

claim: R-loops are most frequently observed at highly transcribed genes but can also be formed at telomeres and near DNA replication forks.
source: R-loops are most frequently observed at highly transcribed genes but can also be formed at telomeres and near DNA replication forks (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a statement about R-loop formation based on established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: Deletion of HPR1 was synthetic lethal when combined with the nse4-4 mutation.
source: Interestingly, deletion of HPR1 was synthetic lethal when combined with the nse4-4 mutation, as evidenced by the growth pattern of haploid spores following sporulation and dissection of a heterozygous diploid strain (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: hpr1Δ smc6-9 double mutants were viable.
source: Although hpr1Δ smc6-9 double mutants were viable, the growth defect associated with the hpr1Δ mutation was strongly exacerbated in the presence of smc6-9 at both permissive and restrictive temperatures (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The growth defect associated with the hpr1Δ mutation was strongly exacerbated in the presence of smc6-9 at both permissive and restrictive temperatures.
source: Although hpr1Δ smc6-9 double mutants were viable, the growth defect associated with the hpr1Δ mutation was strongly exacerbated in the presence of smc6-9 at both permissive and restrictive temperatures (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: smc6-9, nse4-4 and mms21-H202Y alleles experienced synthetic growth defects when combined with sen1-1.
source: smc6-9, nse4-4 and mms21-H202Y alleles also experienced synthetic growth defects when combined with sen1-1 (see 30 °C /32 °C and HU/MMS conditions in Figure 4B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The nse4-4 sen1-1 mutant showed defective proliferation even under normal/unchallenged growth conditions.
source: The nse4-4 sen1-1 mutant showed defective proliferation even under normal/unchallenged growth conditions, consistent with the more severe temperature sensitivity of this allele compared to that of smc6-9 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A significant increase in the numbers of S9.6 foci was detected on chromatin spreads prepared from nse4-4 sen1-1 and hpr1Δ smc6-9 mutants compared to those from single mutant strains.
source: Moreover, we detected a significant increase in the numbers of S9.6 foci on chromatin spreads prepared from nse4-4 sen1-1 and hpr1Δ smc6-9 mutants compared to those from single mutant strains (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: R-loops formed at highly transcribed genes are physiological substrates for the Smc5/6 complex.
source: Taken together, these genetic interactions suggest that R-loop formed at highly transcribed genes are physiological substrates for the Smc5/6 complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from genetic interaction data with sen1-1 and hpr1Δ mutants.

claim: The pol2-M644G mutant exhibits a 10-fold increased ribonucleotide incorporation during DNA replication.
source: Specifically, the pol2-M644G mutant exhibits a 10-fold increased ribonucleotide incorporation during DNA replication (McElhinny et al., 2010) whereas the sen1-3 allele (carrying point mutations in the N-terminal domain of Sen1) impairs the interaction of Sen1 with the replication machinery, thereby increasing R-loop formation in the vicinity of replication forks (Figure 4A; Appanah et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The sen1-3 allele impairs the interaction of Sen1 with the replication machinery, thereby increasing R-loop formation in the vicinity of replication forks.
source: Specifically, the pol2-M644G mutant exhibits a 10-fold increased ribonucleotide incorporation during DNA replication (McElhinny et al., 2010) whereas the sen1-3 allele (carrying point mutations in the N-terminal domain of Sen1) impairs the interaction of Sen1 with the replication machinery, thereby increasing R-loop formation in the vicinity of replication forks (Figure 4A; Appanah et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: No synthetic growth defects were observed in double mutants of pol2-M644G or sen1-3 with smc6-9 and nse4-4 mutations.
source: We did not observe synthetic growth defects in double mutants of these genes with smc6-9 and nse4-4 mutations (Figure 4B), suggesting that DNA replication-associated RNA-DNA hybrid structures are not substrates for the Smc5/6 complex in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: DNA replication-associated RNA-DNA hybrid structures are not substrates for the Smc5/6 complex in vivo.
source: We did not observe synthetic growth defects in double mutants of these genes with smc6-9 and nse4-4 mutations (Figure 4B), suggesting that DNA replication-associated RNA-DNA hybrid structures are not substrates for the Smc5/6 complex in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of genetic interactions with pol2-M644G and sen1-3 mutants.

claim: Double mutant strains combining smc6-9 or nse4-4 mutations with the rat1-1 allele exhibited stronger growth defects than the corresponding single mutants.
source: To this end, we combined smc6-9 and nse4-4 mutations with the rat1-1 allele defective in the 5' to 3' exonuclease activity responsible for TERRA removal (Figure 4A; Luke et al., 2008). The resulting double mutant strains exhibited stronger growth defects than the corresponding single mutants (Figure 4B), indicating a role for the Smc5/6 complex in R-loop metabolism at telomeres.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The Smc5/6 complex has a role in R-loop metabolism at telomeres.
source: The resulting double mutant strains exhibited stronger growth defects than the corresponding single mutants (Figure 4B), indicating a role for the Smc5/6 complex in R-loop metabolism at telomeres.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from genetic interaction data with rat1-1 mutant.

claim: Combining rat1-1 and smc6-9 mutations to sen1-1 phenocopied the sen1-1 smc6-9 double mutant.
source: Combining rat1-1 and smc6-9 mutations to sen1-1 phenocopied the sen1-1 smc6-9 double mutant (Figure 4C), consistent with an involvement of Sen1 in telomeric R-loops metabolism.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Sen1 is involved in telomeric R-loops metabolism.
source: Combining rat1-1 and smc6-9 mutations to sen1-1 phenocopied the sen1-1 smc6-9 double mutant (Figure 4C), consistent with an involvement of Sen1 in telomeric R-loops metabolism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from genetic interaction data.

claim: R-loops formed at highly transcribed genes and telomeres are likely physiological targets for the Smc5/6 complex.
source: Overall, these genetic analyses suggest that R-loops formed at highly transcribed genes and telomeres are likely physiological targets for the Smc5/6 complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic interaction data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Yeast and human Smc5/6 complexes are highly conserved and show strong binding affinities towards DNA substrates that mimic single-stranded (ss)–double-stranded (ds) DNA junctions, supercoiled or catenated DNA, and even branched DNA structures.
source: Extensive research over recent years has revealed that yeast and human Smc5/6 complexes are highly conserved and show strong binding affinities towards DNA substrates that mimic single-stranded (ss)–double-stranded (ds) DNA junctions, supercoiled or catenated DNA, and even branched DNA structures (Serrano et al., 2020; Gutierrez-Escribano et al., 2020; Tanasie et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature including work from the authors' laboratory.

claim: The human SMC5/6 complex can bind short RNA-DNA duplexes in vitro.
source: We have also established that the human SMC5/6 complex can bind short RNA-DNA duplexes in vitro (Serrano et al., 2020), suggesting the enzyme is capable of recognizing the more complex R-loop structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work from the authors' laboratory.

claim: The SMC5/6 complex can bind both R-loop and D-loop structures in EMSA experiments.
source: We observed that the SMC5/6 complex can bind both R-loop and D-loop structures in EMSA experiments, but its specificity for the R-loop structure appeared slightly greater (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: The SMC5/6 complex specificity for the R-loop structure appeared slightly greater than for D-loop structures.
source: We observed that the SMC5/6 complex can bind both R-loop and D-loop structures in EMSA experiments, but its specificity for the R-loop structure appeared slightly greater (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: The SMC5/6 complex can bind the R-loop substrate even at a lower concentration of 6.25 nM and 12.5 nM.
source: For instance, the SMC5/6 complex can bind the R-loop substrate even at a lower concentration of 6.25 nM and 12.5 nM, as evident from the protein/DNA band shift formed at the top of the gel at that concentration of enzyme (lane 2 and 3; Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Little to no binding to D-loops was observed at 6.25 nM and 12.5 nM of SMC5/6 complex.
source: In contrast, we observed little to no binding to D-loops at 6.25 nM and 12.5 nM of SMC5/6 complex (lane 2 and 3; Figure 5D) and visibly moderate binding at the higher concentrations of protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The calculated equilibrium dissociation constant (KD) of the Smc5/6 complex was slightly lower for R-loop substrates than for D-loops.
source: Consistent with this, the calculated equilibrium dissociation constant (KD) of the Smc5/6 complex was slightly lower for R-loop substrates than for D-loops, but the significance of this difference, if any, remains to be established (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The single-stranded DNA part of the R-loop may be important for SMC5/6 complex binding on these structures.
source: The similar range of binding affinities of the SMC5/6 complex for the R-loop and D-loop suggests that the single-stranded DNA part of the R-loop may be important for SMC5/6 complex binding on these structures—a mechanism previously observed for DICER-mediated R-loop resolution (Camino et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the binding data, drawing on a mechanism observed for DICER.

claim: The SMC5/6 complex maintained its binding to R-loops even when challenged with 100-fold excess double-stranded DNA analogue.
source: Importantly, we observed that the SMC5/6 complex maintained its binding to R-loops even when challenged with 100-fold excess double-stranded DNA analogue (i.e., Poly[d(I-C)]), a behavior not observed with D-loops (lane 11–13 Figure 5C vs lane 10–12 Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: The binding of the Smc5/6 complex to R-loops is more resilient to challenge by a competitor substrate than the interaction of the enzyme to D-loops.
source: These data suggest that the binding of the Smc5/6 complex to R-loops is more resilient to challenge by a competitor substrate than the interaction of the enzyme to D-loops.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the competitive EMSA data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: The SMC5/6 complex can efficiently associate with R-loops.
source: Together, our EMSA experiments indicate that the SMC5/6 complex can efficiently associate with R-loops.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EMSA experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Multimeric condensin bound R-loop substrates with high efficiency.
source: While multimeric condensin bound R-loop substrates with high efficiency, similar concentrations of the enzyme in monomeric form failed to bind R-loop substrates in EMSA experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–F.

claim: Monomeric condensin failed to bind R-loop substrates in EMSA experiments.
source: While multimeric condensin bound R-loop substrates with high efficiency, similar concentrations of the enzyme in monomeric form failed to bind R-loop substrates in EMSA experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–F.

claim: The ability to bind R-loops is not an intrinsic property of monomeric condensin.
source: This result suggests that the ability to bind R-loops is not an intrinsic property of monomeric condensin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the condensin binding experiments.

claim: RNase H2 is the only RNase H enzyme that acts throughout the cell cycle.
source: RNase H1 and RNase H2 are the primary enzymes responsible for the removal of R-loops in chromosomes, but recent studies suggest that RNase H2 is the only one that acts throughout the cell cycle (Lockhart et al., 2019; Zimmer and Koshland, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A remarkably strong genetic interaction was observed when combining Smc5/6 complex mutations with RNase H2 enzyme inactivation.
source: Consistent with this, we also observed a remarkably strong genetic interaction when combining Smc5/6 complex mutations with RNase H2 enzyme inactivation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Human RNase H2 was able to cleave the radiolabeled RNA in a time and concentration-dependent manner.
source: We first confirmed that human RNase H2 was able to cleave the radiolabeled RNA in a time and concentration-dependent manner (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: The purified RNase H2 enzyme was not active on a D-loop structure.
source: We also observed that the purified RNase H2 enzyme was not active on a D-loop structure, thereby demonstrating the specificity of the enzyme in our reaction conditions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The SMC5/6 complex did not induce degradation of the RNA moiety or otherwise affect the stability of the R-loop structure in the absence of RNase H2.
source: Next, we incubated increasing concentrations of the SMC5/6 complex with the R-loop substrate in the absence of RNase H2. Under these conditions, the complex did not induce degradation of the RNA moiety or otherwise affect the stability of the R-loop structure (lanes 2–6; Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In the presence of low levels of RNase H2 enzyme, the SMC5/6 complex induced a major stimulation of R-loop degradation.
source: However, in the presence of low levels of RNase H2 enzyme, the same concentrations of SMC5/6 complex induced a major stimulation of R-loop degradation. This led to a rapid accumulation of radiolabeled product at the bottom of the gel (lanes 8–12; Figure 6C), reflecting the nucleolytic processing of the RNA moiety within the R-loop by RNase H2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The stimulation of RNase H2 activity by the SMC5/6 complex was concentration-dependent.
source: The stimulation of RNase H2 activity by the SMC5/6 complex was concentration-dependent and evident even at the lowest concentration of the SMC5/6 complex tested in this experiment (1.25 nM, lane 8; Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: No detectable physical interaction was found connecting the SMC5/6 complex and RNase H2 in pull-down assays.
source: To test the possibility that the SMC5/6 complex modulates RNase H2 activity by direct binding, we performed an in vitro pull-down assay and found no detectable physical interaction connecting these proteins, a result further confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation assays from yeast extracts (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: The promotion of R-loop degradation by the SMC5/6 complex does not depend on this enzyme establishing a strong physical interaction with RNase H2.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the promotion of R-loop degradation by the SMC5/6 complex does not depend on this enzyme establishing a strong physical interaction with RNase H2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pull-down and co-IP experiments.

claim: Previous genetic experiments have supported a role for the Smc5/6 complex in the natural regulation of TERRA levels at telomeres.
source: While previous genetic experiments have supported a role for the Smc5/6 complex in the natural regulation of TERRA levels at telomeres (Lafuente-Barquero et al., 2017; Moradi-Fard et al., 2016), our study reports the first demonstration that Smc5/6 complex activity is essential for the removal of unscheduled R-loops from the genome.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: This study reports the first demonstration that Smc5/6 complex activity is essential for the removal of unscheduled R-loops from the genome.
source: While previous genetic experiments have supported a role for the Smc5/6 complex in the natural regulation of TERRA levels at telomeres (Lafuente-Barquero et al., 2017; Moradi-Fard et al., 2016), our study reports the first demonstration that Smc5/6 complex activity is essential for the removal of unscheduled R-loops from the genome.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current study's findings.

claim: Non-physiological R-loops represent the most toxic and damaging source of RNA-DNA hybrids for genome stability.
source: This discovery is significant because non-physiological R-loops represent the most toxic and damaging source of RNA-DNA hybrids for genome stability (Crossley et al., 2019; Brambati et al., 2020; Petermann et al., 2022) and failure to remove these structures exacts a heavy toll on cell fitness.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Failure to remove non-physiological R-loops exacts a heavy toll on cell fitness.
source: This discovery is significant because non-physiological R-loops represent the most toxic and damaging source of RNA-DNA hybrids for genome stability (Crossley et al., 2019; Brambati et al., 2020; Petermann et al., 2022) and failure to remove these structures exacts a heavy toll on cell fitness.
evidence: This is a general statement about the consequences of R-loop accumulation supported by citations.

claim: This study demonstrates for the first time that the Smc5/6 complex can directly recognize R-loops.
source: Moreover, we demonstrate for the first time that the Smc5/6 complex can directly recognize R-loops, suggesting an early role in the detection and repair of these structures in vivo (see model in Figure 7).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current study's findings, supported by the EMSA data in Figure 5.

claim: The Smc5/6 complex has an early role in the detection and repair of R-loop structures in vivo.
source: Moreover, we demonstrate for the first time that the Smc5/6 complex can directly recognize R-loops, suggesting an early role in the detection and repair of these structures in vivo (see model in Figure 7).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings, illustrated in the model in Figure 7.

claim: The Smc5/6 complex has been shown by chromatin immunoprecipitation to accumulate at sites that are common R-loop enrichment zones on chromosomes, including the rDNA locus, telomeres, and highly transcribed/difficult-to-replicate chromosomal loci.
source: Consistent with this suggestion, the Smc5/6 complex has been shown by chromatin immunoprecipitation to accumulate at sites that are common R-loop enrichment zones on chromosomes, including the rDNA locus, telomeres, and highly transcribed/difficult-to-replicate chromosomal loci (Diman et al., 2023; Jeppsson et al., 2023; Jeppsson et al., 2014; Pebernard et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Inactivation of Smc5/6 components leads to an increase in R-loop formation at rDNA locus, telomeres, and highly transcribed loci in the absence of RNase H enzyme activity.
source: We showed that inactivation of Smc5/6 components leads to an increase in R-loop formation at several of these loci in the absence of RNase H enzyme activity, a result that aligns nicely with Smc5/6 complex localization in live cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the DRIP data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Synthetic or enhancement phenotypes involving non-null alleles reflect the contribution of two mutations to the same cellular process, but not necessarily or exclusively in the same molecular pathway.
source: Synthetic or enhancement phenotypes involving non-null alleles reflect the contribution of two mutations to the same cellular process, but not necessarily or exclusively in the same molecular pathway (i.e., interactions 'within pathways' and 'between pathways;' reviewed in Huang and Sternberg, 1995; Boone et al., 2007; Roth et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about genetic interaction interpretation supported by citations to review literature.

claim: The Smc5/6 complex acts at two distinct levels in the cellular response to R-loop formation: within and between pathways.
source: We favor a model where the Smc5/6 complex acts at two distinct levels –within and between pathways– in the cellular response to R-loop formation (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors to explain their findings, illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Smc5/6 contributes to RNase H-dependent removal of RNA-DNA hybrids from genomic DNA.
source: First, Smc5/6 contributes to RNase H-dependent removal of RNA-DNA hybrids from genomic DNA, as shown in Figures 1 and 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The Smc5/6 role in RNA-DNA hybrid removal is substantial but not as extensive as that of RNase H enzymes.
source: In the execution of this function, the Smc5/6 role is substantial but not as extensive as that of RNase H enzymes (more on this below).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the relative contributions of Smc5/6 and RNase H based on the experimental data.

claim: The Smc5/6 complex plays an important role in the maintenance of DNA replication fork stability.
source: Second, the Smc5/6 complex plays an important role in the maintenance of DNA replication fork stability, as previously established (Peng and Zhao, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The Smc5/6 complex role in replication fork stability is crucial for cellular fitness in the presence of elevated R-loop levels because these structures often disrupt replication fork progression and can lead to fork collapse.
source: This role is crucial for cellular fitness in the presence of elevated R-loop levels because these structures often disrupt replication fork progression and can lead to fork collapse (Crossley et al., 2019; Brambati et al., 2020; Petermann et al., 2022; Kemiha et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Combining sen1-1 or sen1-3 alleles with rnh1Δ rnh201Δ mutations leads to synthetic lethality.
source: For instance, past genetic interaction studies have shown that combining sen1-1 or sen1-3 alleles with rnh1Δ rnh201Δ mutations leads to synthetic lethality (Appanah et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Inactivation of the THO complex induces a substantial increase in RNA-DNA hybrids in cells defective in RNase H activity.
source: Likewise, inactivation of the THO complex induces a substantial increase in RNA-DNA hybrids in cells defective in RNase H activity (Yang et al., 2021), similar to our observation with nse4-4 rnh1Δ rnh201Δ and smc6-9 rnh1Δ rnh201Δ mutant strains (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature and comparison to the current study's data.

claim: The pattern of synthetic enhancements when inactivating effectors of RNA-DNA hybrid metabolism is consistent with multiple mechanisms acting independently to promote the removal of toxic or unscheduled R-loops from eukaryotic genomes.
source: This pattern of synthetic enhancements when inactivating effectors of RNA-DNA hybrid metabolism is consistent with multiple mechanisms acting independently to promote the removal of toxic or unscheduled R-loops from eukaryotic genomes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the genetic interaction patterns observed in this and prior studies.

claim: RNase H1 shows little enzymatic activity under basal conditions and requires stimulation by ancillary factors, such as RPA, to achieve maximal R-loop degradation.
source: Hints of a potential mechanism of action come from the observation that one of the enzymes responsible for R-loop degradation, RNase H1, shows little enzymatic activity under basal conditions and requires stimulation by ancillary factors, such as RPA, to achieve maximal R-loop degradation (Nguyen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: RNase H2 might require the assistance of a separate stimulatory factor to achieve maximal catalytic efficiency.
source: It therefore seems plausible that RNase H2 might also require the assistance of a separate stimulatory factor to achieve maximal catalytic efficiency.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on analogy to RNase H1.

claim: RNase H2 activity can be stimulated effectively, and in a dose-dependent manner by the Smc5/6 complex.
source: Testing this notion in a reconstituted R-loop degradation assay confirmed the model that RNase H2 activity can be stimulated effectively, and in a dose-dependent manner by the Smc5/6 complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the in vitro degradation assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: RNase H1 shows very little RNA degradation activity in the absence of RPA.
source: The two RNase H enzymes differ, however, in that RNase H1 shows very little RNA degradation activity in the absence of RPA (Nguyen et al., 2017), whereas RNase H2 is moderately active as an R-loop degrading enzyme at basal state (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: RNase H2 is moderately active as an R-loop degrading enzyme at basal state.
source: The two RNase H enzymes differ, however, in that RNase H1 shows very little RNA degradation activity in the absence of RPA (Nguyen et al., 2017), whereas RNase H2 is moderately active as an R-loop degrading enzyme at basal state (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Smc5/6 complex is probably not required to stimulate RNase H2 activity in all contexts in vivo but is likely more important in challenging environments where R-loops are highly abundant or otherwise difficult to degrade effectively by RNase H2 alone.
source: The implication for the Smc5/6 complex is that it is probably not required to stimulate RNase H2 activity in all contexts in vivo but is likely more important in challenging environments where R-loops are highly abundant or otherwise difficult to degrade effectively by RNase H2 alone.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the biochemical and genetic data.

claim: The repertoire of genomic lesions that are substrates for RNase H2 and the Smc5/6 complex in vivo is not fully overlapping.
source: Taken together, our genetic analyses indicate that the repertoire of genomic lesions that are substrates for RNase H2 and the Smc5/6 complex in vivo is not fully overlapping.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic interaction data showing specificity for certain types of R-loops.

claim: An RNase H2 stimulatory role for the Smc5/6 complex provides a cellular capacity/buffer to address substantial fluctuations in the total load of RNA-DNA hybrids produced under physiological and non-physiological conditions.
source: An RNase H2 stimulatory role for the Smc5/6 complex is compelling because it provides a cellular capacity/buffer to address substantial fluctuations in the total load of RNA-DNA hybrids produced under physiological and non-physiological conditions (Mackay et al., 2020; Petermann et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Reducing the total load of RNA-DNA hybrids or altering its sources of origin is expected to modify the requirement for the Smc5/6 complex in R-loop metabolism.
source: Consequently, reducing the total load of RNA-DNA hybrids or altering its sources of origin is expected to modify the requirement for the Smc5/6 complex in R-loop metabolism (Lafuente-Barquero et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model and supported by a citation.

claim: RNase H1 is strongly stimulated by a ssDNA binding protein, RPA.
source: This is a question for a future study, but it has not escaped our attention that RNase H1 is strongly stimulated by a ssDNA binding protein, RPA (Nguyen et al., 2017), a biochemical property also encoded in the Smc5/6 complex (Serrano et al., 2020; Roy and D'Amours, 2011; Roy et al., 2011; Roy et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The Smc5/6 complex has ssDNA binding activity.
source: This is a question for a future study, but it has not escaped our attention that RNase H1 is strongly stimulated by a ssDNA binding protein, RPA (Nguyen et al., 2017), a biochemical property also encoded in the Smc5/6 complex (Serrano et al., 2020; Roy and D'Amours, 2011; Roy et al., 2011; Roy et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work from the authors' laboratory.

claim: The Smc5/6 complex plays a vital role in promoting RPA binding and maintenance at ssDNA during homologous recombination.
source: Separate from this possibility, the Smc5/6 complex plays a vital role in promoting RPA binding and maintenance at ssDNA during homologous recombination (Tanasie et al., 2022), a function that could indirectly stimulate RNase H1 activity and R-loop repair (Nguyen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The Smc5/6 complex function in promoting RPA binding could indirectly stimulate RNase H1 activity and R-loop repair.
source: Separate from this possibility, the Smc5/6 complex plays a vital role in promoting RPA binding and maintenance at ssDNA during homologous recombination (Tanasie et al., 2022), a function that could indirectly stimulate RNase H1 activity and R-loop repair (Nguyen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a potential indirect mechanism.

claim: The Smc5/6 complex has been thought of primarily as a genome stability factor associated with the repair of DSBs, recovery of stalled replication forks, telomeric length maintenance, and virus restriction.
source: Up to now, the Smc5/6 complex has been thought of primarily as a genome stability factor associated with the repair of DSBs, recovery of stalled replication forks, telomeric length maintenance, and virus restriction (Peng and Zhao, 2023).
evidence: This is a statement about the current understanding of Smc5/6 function supported by a citation.

claim: Failure to execute Smc5/6 complex functions generates toxic recombination intermediates in vivo.
source: While it is not evident why the Smc5/6 complex would be involved in such a diverse and loosely connected group of cellular functions, it is nevertheless clear that failure to execute these functions generates toxic recombination intermediates in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement about the consequences of Smc5/6 dysfunction based on established knowledge.

claim: The Smc5/6 complex binds to ssDNA intermediates and branched/structured substrates at DNA repair sites.
source: Under normal circumstances, the Smc5/6 complex binds to ssDNA intermediates and branched/structured substrates at DNA repair sites and the association of the complex to these DNA intermediates provides a platform for repair factors to resolve toxic DNA lesions (Serrano et al., 2020; Gutierrez-Escribano et al., 2020; Tanasie et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature including work from the authors' laboratory.

claim: The association of the Smc5/6 complex to DNA intermediates provides a platform for repair factors to resolve toxic DNA lesions.
source: Under normal circumstances, the Smc5/6 complex binds to ssDNA intermediates and branched/structured substrates at DNA repair sites and the association of the complex to these DNA intermediates provides a platform for repair factors to resolve toxic DNA lesions (Serrano et al., 2020; Gutierrez-Escribano et al., 2020; Tanasie et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature including work from the authors' laboratory.

claim: Most of the nuclear processes involving the Smc5/6 complex involve the formation of RNA-DNA hybrids in one form or another.
source: It is interesting to note that most of the nuclear processes outlined above involve the formation of RNA-DNA hybrids in one form or another (Brambati et al., 2020; Petermann et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an observation about the commonality of RNA-DNA hybrids in Smc5/6-related processes, supported by citations.

claim: The function uncovered for the Smc5/6 complex in RNA-DNA metabolism may be a unifying role that explains its involvement in such a diverse repertoire of cellular functions.
source: As such, the function we uncovered for the Smc5/6 complex in RNA-DNA metabolism may be a unifying role that explains its involvement in such a diverse repertoire of cellular functions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader significance of the findings.

claim: The Smc5/6 complex binds strongly to RNA-DNA hybrid structures formed during active gene transcription and telomere length regulation.
source: In conclusion, our work demonstrates a direct and active involvement of the Smc5/6 complex in the removal of R-loops from eukaryotic chromosomes. We showed the Smc5/6 complex binds strongly to RNA-DNA hybrid structures formed during active gene transcription and telomere length regulation, and subsequently promotes the removal of these toxic structures via the stimulation of RNase H2 enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: The Smc5/6 complex promotes the removal of toxic R-loop structures via the stimulation of RNase H2 enzymatic activity.
source: We showed the Smc5/6 complex binds strongly to RNA-DNA hybrid structures formed during active gene transcription and telomere length regulation, and subsequently promotes the removal of these toxic structures via the stimulation of RNase H2 enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: This work uncovered a previously unanticipated contribution of the Smc5/6 complex in genome stability with important ramifications for the health and disease of all eukaryotic organisms.
source: This work uncovered a previously unanticipated contribution of the Smc5/6 complex in genome stability with important ramifications for the health and disease of all eukaryotic organisms.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance and novelty of the findings.
